food.text: Mesopotamian settlers were among the first people to make beer and wine. Their homeland lay within the Tigris–Euphrates river system, in the northern part of the Fertile Crescent.

Sumerian farmers along the valleys of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers grew an abundance of grain and other crops. The surplus enabled them to form urban settlements, and the world's earliest known texts come from the Sumerian cities of Uruk and Jemdet Nasr.

The unpredictable Mesopotamian weather was often hard on farmers, and frequent floods ravaged entire cities. Because crops were often ruined, farmers kept backup sources of food such as cows and lambs.
Farming in the Mesopotamian region required particular skills. As a result, farmers did not generally depend on slaves to do the work.
Over time the southernmost parts of Sumerian Mesopotamia suffered from increased salinity of the soils. This led to a slow urban decline and moved power to Akkad, further north.

Isin had a huge problem maintaining access to its water sources. Larsa's kings Abisare (c. 1841–1830 BCE) and Sumuel (c. 1830–1801 BCE) took steps to cut off Isin's access to canals completely by rerouting them into Larsa, which later flourished with huge building and agricultural projects.

art.text: Mesopotamian art from the periods before the Neo-Assyrian Empire survives in several forms. These include cylinder seals, relatively small figures in the round, and reliefs of various sizes. There were also cheap plaques of moulded pottery made for the home, some religious and some apparently not.

The Burney Relief is an unusual, elaborate and relatively large terracotta plaque, about 20 x 15 inches. It shows a naked winged goddess with the feet of a bird of prey, flanked by attendant owls and lions. It comes from the 18th or 19th century BC and may have been moulded.

At Uruk, artists made small votive animal figurines in a style that mixed naturalistic and abstract elements. They aimed to capture the spiritual essence of the animal rather than an anatomically exact figure. Many were found at Uruk Level III, around 3000 BCE, and were offered to the goddess Inanna in return for her favor.

The use of animal figures as votive offerings, rather than human figures, probably replaces a ritual act of animal sacrifice. The figurine makes the act eternal by leaving the image of the sacrificed animal in the temple.

Archaeologist Jesse Millek showed that trade in Cypriot pottery in the southern Levant largely ended around 1300 BC, and trade in Mycenaean pottery ended around 1250 BC. Both ended before the destruction of about 1200 BC, so that destruction cannot have caused them.

The Burney Relief is a large terracotta plaque, about 20 by 15 inches, showing a naked winged goddess with the feet of a bird of prey. She is flanked by owls and lions. It dates from the 18th or 19th century BC and may have been moulded.
Hittite art includes a number of large recumbent lions carved in stone. The largest is the Lion of Babylon statue at Babylon, if it is indeed Hittite.

war.text: The Stele of the Vultures, made at the end of the Early Dynastic III period (2600–2350 BC), commemorates the victory of Eannatum of Lagash over the neighbouring rival city of Umma. It is the oldest monument in the world that celebrates a massacre.

Gilgamesh, an Early Dynastic II king of Uruk around 2600 BC, was commended for military exploits against Humbaba, guardian of the Cedar Mountain. Later poems and songs celebrated him and claimed he was two-thirds god and only one-third human.

Around 2334 BC, the long phase of warring Mesopotamian city-states came to an end. Sargon of Akkad rose to power and founded the Akkadian Empire, which followed directly after the Early Dynastic Period.

The Late Bronze Age collapse, in the late 13th to early 12th century BC, was sudden and violent. Most theories involve the violent destruction of cities and towns, including invasions by the Sea Peoples. The Hittite Empire, spanning Anatolia and the Levant, collapsed. At Ugarit, the last king Ammurapi wrote that enemy ships had come, his cities were burned and the invaders 'did evil things in my country'. Archaeologists found thirty-two arrowheads in one residential area alone, along with lance heads, javelin heads, daggers and a sword scattered through houses and streets, which shows the city was ruined by an assault, not an earthquake.

Royal inscriptions from Lagash record wars against other Lower Mesopotamian city-states and against distant kingdoms such as Mari, Subartu and Elam. King Eannatum of Lagash was able to defeat Mari and Elam around 2450 BC.

The Akkadian Empire eventually disintegrated due to economic decline, climate change and civil war. Attacks by the Gutians from the Zagros Mountains followed. Sumer rose again under the Third Dynasty of Ur, which ejected the Gutians from southern Mesopotamia in 2161 BC.

Hammurabi of Babylon created a short-lived empire, succeeding the earlier Akkadian Empire, Third Dynasty of Ur and Old Assyrian Empire. It rapidly fell apart after his death, and Babylonia reverted to a small kingdom centered around the city of Babylon.
Ramesses II of Egypt campaigned against the wandering Shasu, pursuing them as far as Moab. There he established a fortress, after a near defeat at the Battle of Kadesh.

Around 2358 BC, Lugal-zage-si, king of Uruk and Umma, seized most of Lower Mesopotamia. Some years later, around 2350 BC, Enshakushanna of Uruk seized Kish and imprisoned its king Embi-Ishtar. These conflicts show a trend toward stronger states dominating larger territories.

Egyptian evidence shows that from the reign of Horemheb, wandering Shasu were more problematic than the earlier ʿApiru. During the reign of Merneptah, the Shasu threatened the "Way of Horus" north from Gaza.

Dating the Battle of Megiddo is uncertain. Egyptian lunar observations have been used to suggest that the accession of Thutmose III, the pharaoh of that battle, was in 1490 BC or even 1505 BC, rather than the currently accepted 1470 BC.
war.source_title: Chronology of the ancient Near East

literature.text: The world's earliest known texts come from the Sumerian cities of Uruk and Jemdet Nasr. They date to between about 3350 and 2500 BC, following a long period of proto-writing.

Bronze Age cultures were the first to develop writing. According to archaeological evidence, Mesopotamia, which used cuneiform script, and Egypt, which used hieroglyphs, developed the earliest practical writing systems.

The Akkadians, Assyrians, Babylonians and Eblaites were the first Semitic-speaking peoples to use writing. They used the cuneiform script that the Sumerians had developed around 3500 BC, and the first writings in Akkadian date from about 2800 BC.
Akkadian gradually replaced Sumerian as the spoken language of Mesopotamia around the turn of the third and second millennium BC. The precise timeframe is a matter of debate.

The third phase of the Early Dynastic Period saw an expansion in the use of writing and the appearance of the first royal inscriptions. Its earlier part is the period of the royal tombs of Ur and the archives of Fara, ancient Shuruppak, and Abu Salabikh.

Texts written entirely in Old Akkadian date from about 2500 BC, and the language's use peaked under Sargon of Akkad. Even then, most administrative tablets continued to be written in Sumerian, the language used by the scribes.

The Babylonian state kept written Akkadian for official use, even though its Amorite founders spoke a Northwest Semitic language and its Kassite successors spoke a language isolate. It also kept the Sumerian language in sacred texts for the Babylonian religion.
The earliest known Akkadian inscription was found on a bowl at Ur. It is addressed to the very early king Meskiang-nunna of Ur by his queen Gan-saman, who is thought to have been from Akkad.

Cuneiform writing rose in the Uruk and Jemdet Nasr periods, but the rulers who followed in the Early Bronze Age are known mostly from scant contemporary sources. One example is En-me-barage-si, and this scarcity makes absolute dates hard to assign.
literature.source_title: Chronology of the ancient Near East

science.text: Mesopotamian mathematics and science were built on a sexagesimal, or base 60, number system. This is the source of the 60-minute hour, the 24-hour day and the 360-degree circle. The same mathematics was instrumental in early map-making.

Mesopotamia is credited with inspiring the invention of the wheel, the planting of the first cereal crops and the development of cursive script. It also gave rise to early mathematics, astronomy and agriculture. It is recognised as the cradle of some of the world's earliest civilizations.

The earliest identifiable predecessors to modern science date to the Bronze Age in Egypt and Mesopotamia, c. 3000 to 1200 BCE. Their contributions to mathematics, astronomy and medicine later entered and shaped Greek natural philosophy.
The Sumerian calendar was lunisolar. It divided a lunar month into three seven-day weeks. It belonged to a scientific tradition built on the sexagesimal numeral system.

Thirteen Egyptian New Kingdom lunar observations are used to lock the accession of Ramsesses II to 1279 BC. The Assyrian eponym list is accurate to one year only back to 1132 BC, so Near East chronology for the century or so before that is anchored to Ramsesses II.
science.source_title: Chronology of the ancient Near East

science.text: Towards the end of the Uruk period, cylinder seals depict sleds less and less, and begin to show the first vehicles that appear to be on wheels. There were certainly chariots in southern Mesopotamia at the start of the 3rd millennium BC, with solid block wheels, since spokes were not invented until about 2000 BC.

The Egyptians and Mesopotamians of the Bronze Age did not have the words or concepts of "science" and "nature". Even so, their work in mathematics, astronomy and medicine later found a place in Greek and medieval science. Writing gave the earliest written records in the history of science.

The lunar observations that fix Near East dates come with problems. Their location is usually assumed to be Memphis, and two are known to have been made on the 1st lunar day. The Egyptian calendar of the period is not fully known, especially how intercalary months were handled.
science.source_title: Chronology of the ancient Near East

science.text: Dating the Early Bronze Age of southern Mesopotamia is hard. There is no dendrochronology, few astronomical correlations and few well-stratified radiocarbon sequences. The result is a "floating" chronology without firm absolute dates.
science.source_title: Chronology of the ancient Near East

science.text: Carnelian beads etched with a white design were found in Ur tombs dating to 2600 to 2450. They were probably imported from the Indus Valley. They were made by an acid-etching technique developed by the Harappans.

Radiocarbon dates from the final destruction of Ebla favour the middle chronology, with the fall of Babylon and Aleppo at c. 1595 BC. They seem to discount the ultra-low chronology, which puts the same event at c. 1499 BC. This is not presented as a decisive argument.
science.source_title: Chronology of the ancient Near East

politics.text: Around 2300 BCE, Sargon of Akkad defeated King Lugal-zage-si of Uruk, the most powerful king in southern Mesopotamia. According to copies of Sargon's inscriptions, the defeated king was captured, forced to wear a yoke, and paraded in Sargon's triumphal procession in Nippur. Sargon then subjugated the other Sumerian cities and replaced the independent Sumero-Akkadian city-states with a centralized government. The Akkadian Empire is often seen as the first empire in world history.

From about 2900 to 2350 BC, Mesopotamia was divided among small city-states such as Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Umma, and Nippur. Despite this political fragmentation, they shared a relatively homogeneous material culture. The period ended with unification under Sargon, the first monarch of the Akkadian Empire.

The Kassite dynasty ruled the kingdom of Babylon between 1595 and 1155 BC, making it the longest known dynasty of that state. Despite their foreign origin, the Kassite kings did not change Babylon's ancestral traditions and instead brought order after the turbulence that ended the first dynasty.

Around the late 13th to early 12th century BC, the Hittite Empire collapsed, while the Middle Assyrian Empire and the New Kingdom of Egypt survived in weakened forms. The Phoenicians enjoyed increased autonomy and power as the military presence of Egypt and Assyria waned.

Naram-Sin, the grandson of Sargon, declared himself a living god and took the title "King of the Four Quarters". It is believed he was deified after crushing a great revolt in Lower Mesopotamia. His inscription on the Great Revolt lists the captured enemy leaders and soldiers killed by the hundreds or even thousands. The rebellious cities were destroyed, and Kish was deliberately flooded.

When the Assyrian ruler Ashur-uballit I broke free from Mitanni rule in 1365 BC, it began a multi-secular confrontation between northern and southern Mesopotamia. Babylon and Assyria became rivals for centuries.

Tukulti-Ninurta I of Assyria invaded and devastated Babylon in a confrontation with Kashtiliash IV, sacking the capital and deporting thousands of people. He had his victory described in the Epic of Tukulti-Ninurta and proclaimed himself king of Babylon.
Royal inscriptions from Lagash record wars against other city-states and distant kingdoms such as Mari, Subartu and Elam. They show that king Eannatum of Lagash defeated Mari and Elam around 2450 BC.

Kara-hardash, a Babylonian king with an Assyrian mother, took the throne in 1333 BC but was assassinated shortly thereafter. His grandfather Ashur-uballit reacted by invading Babylon and putting another grandson, Kurigalzu II, on the throne.

By the mid-third millennium BC, many states and cities in Mesopotamia were ruled or dominated by Akkadian-speaking Semites. The list includes Kish, Ur, Uruk and Nippur, and also Dilmun, to the south of Mesopotamia.

The Elamite king Kidin-Hutran, possibly in solidarity with the Kassite kings to whom he was linked by marriage, devastated Nippur. Assyrian-imposed rulers in Babylon were deposed one after another until 1217 BC.

Evidence at Ugarit shows that its destruction came after the reign of Merneptah and even after the fall of Chancellor Bay in 1192 BC. The city was destroyed in an assault, though the attacker is unknown. Tablets were found baked in the fire, and in the Ville sud thirty-two arrowheads, daggers, lance and javelin heads lay scattered through the houses and streets. Its last Bronze Age king, Ammurapi, a contemporary of the last-known Hittite king Suppiluliuma II, wrote that enemy ships had come, his cities were burned and the enemy did evil things in his country.

philosophy.text: Canaanite religion was polytheistic, with a pantheon headed by the god El and his consort Asherah. Other significant deities included Baal, Anat, Astarte, Dagon, and Rešep, who was the god of plague and of healing. Its myths included divine battles and cycles of death and rebirth: in the Baal Cycle, Mot swallows Baal and sends him to the underworld, and Anat attacks Mot with a knife, grinds him up into pieces, and scatters him far and wide.

Hammurabi, ruler of Babylon, claimed to be a descendant of the moon god Sin. In the ancient world, religious myths were used to strengthen monarchy, and the Egyptian Pharaoh similarly claimed to be the son of the sun god Ra.

Babylonian astronomers were adept at mathematics and could predict eclipses and solstices. Scholars thought that everything in astronomy had some purpose, and most of it related to religion and omens. The origins of astronomy as well as astrology date from this time.

Giorgio Buccellati believes the origins of philosophy can be traced to early Mesopotamian wisdom. That wisdom took the forms of dialectic, dialogues, epic poetry, folklore, hymns, lyrics, prose works and proverbs.

Ashur, patron deity of the city of Assur, was in constant rivalry with Marduk, the patron deity of Babylon, who emerged from about the 19th century BC. In Assyria, Ashur eventually superseded Marduk, even becoming the husband of Ishtar.

The Ugaritic texts, found near Ras Shamra in Syria and dated around 1275 BCE, are the most substantial source on Canaanite religion. Over three hundred of them record myths and legends, incantations, prayers, hymns, deity lists, ritual prescriptions, liturgies, and omen texts.

The earliest evidence of Canaanite religion comes from the Ebla tablets, found at Tell Mardikh, Syria, and dated to the second half of the 3rd millennium BCE. They include lists of offerings to primary deities of the Canaanite pantheon: El, Baal and Dagon.

Until excavation of Ras Shamra, known in antiquity as Ugarit, began in 1928, scholars knew little about Canaanite religious practice. Papyrus documents in the Levant often decayed in the humid Mediterranean climate, so the Bible became the primary source of information on ancient Canaanite religion.

At Emar, a priest's house held a library of literary and lexical texts in the Mesopotamian tradition, along with ritual texts for local cults. Unlike the tablets of other cities, most Emar tablets were of the thirteenth century BC and recorded private transactions rather than royal business.

Canaanite families typically focused on veneration of the dead in the form of household gods and goddesses, the Elohim, while acknowledging deities such as Baal and El. Offerings of food and drink were made to the dead to ensure that they would not trouble the living, and the dead were sometimes asked for help. Kings also played a religious role, and in ceremonies like the hieros gamos of the New Year may have been revered as gods.

culture.text: Mesopotamian religion was polytheistic and worshipped around 2,400 different deities. Many of them were tied to a specific state such as Sumer, Akkad, Assyria or Babylonia, or to a particular city.

Akkadian gradually replaced Sumerian as the spoken language of Mesopotamia around the turn of the 3rd and 2nd millennium BC. Sumerian lived on, though, as a sacred, ceremonial, literary and scientific language in Babylonia and Assyria until the 1st century AD.

In the 3rd millennium BC, Mesopotamian objects of worship were personified and became an expansive cast of divinities with particular functions. Earlier worship had focused on forces of nature as providers of sustenance.

Traditionally, the major religious center of all Mesopotamia was the city of Nippur, where the god Enlil was supreme. It remained so until Babylon replaced it during the reign of Hammurabi in the mid-18th century BC.

Sumerian and Akkadian peoples had worshipped some form of mother goddess, Ninhursag, since the Ubaid Period. Mesopotamian religion is thought to have influenced later faiths, including Canaanite and Israelite, Aramean, and ancient Greek religion.

Babylonia kept Sumerian for the sacred texts of its religion, even though its founders were Northwest Semitic-speaking Amorites and its later rulers were Kassites. Akkadian remained the written language for official use, as it did in Assyria.
